doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Parents' songs, minstrel shows and opinions on today's music
summary: The semi-classical duets his parents sang, the 'Yes We Have No Bananas' minstrel show night, and Conniff's view that there has always been great, frivolous and junk music, rap included.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: The songs that they were playing for you, they were probably considered popular music of that day, were they mostly vocal songs that they had, that you would sing along to?

You know that’s a very interesting question because as I think about it, the music that I used to hear them play and sing, I can remember one, there was one thing that my mother would play, and she would sing like a little soprano lead and my dad would sing like a little obbligato tenor part. And I can’t remember what the piece was, but it was some semi-classical piece, and they used to do that sort of thing. But then you know sometimes people will come up to me like now, in this period of time that we’re doing this interview, I’ll do an interview and someone will say like, “don’t you think some of the music today is really dumb?” You know, and I remember one night they came home and they used to have minstrel shows in those days. And one night they came home from a minstrel show, and my dad was singing, “yes we have no bananas — we have no bananas today.” You know and I mean how dumb can a song be? And so it’s always been that way. There’s been great music and then there’s been very, like frivolous music you know, and then there’s been junk, like that isn’t even music, like rap is that music you know?
It’s rhythm with some story and rhymes and stuff. And music hasn’t changed a lot from what I used to be exposed to.

I think you said a very important thing when you talked about how the ump-chick of your father playing instilled that rhythm in you. Because you can hear that in your arrangements. Do you think that’s one of the keys to what’s made your arranging so successful? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
